name: Hana Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Hana, 58, a junior developer at a tech company that makes booking software for sports clubs. I earned a two-year college diploma after years doing club accounts, and I still ask a senior to check my fixes to member payments. I like making the registration screen clear for a volunteer working the door. I use AI now and then to suggest test cases, but I run them against actual fee records.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does this job support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ben repairs garden tools for a workshop, and our children are grown. My pay is typical for a developer, we have a mortgage, and about four months of expenses saved. His workshop hours are steady, and there are some similar software jobs nearby, though I am still a junior. Retirement is in sight, but we have not checked what our actual income would be if either of us stopped work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau still leaves a club treasurer needing to know which member paid. A child should not be turned away from practice because a screen forgot a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think both wages are safe in this picture. Four months saved will cover a broken boiler, though it will not settle our retirement question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing registrations with actual receipts and ask my senior to review a fee fix. I’d keep our 100 monthly savings transfer while both wages arrive. In the first year I’d use AI only for harmless test ideas, not member names or card details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this year’s work and mortgage. I still want real retirement figures before we make plans for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which member payment did you fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A volunteer at the door showed me a member marked unpaid after a bank delay. I found the payment and printed a corrected list before the next session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rent the spare room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben and I would keep the spare bedroom ready for the children’s visits. We would not count renting it out just because a property advert promises easy money.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking club fees.
I would use **actual receipts** before a child loses a place.
think: I expect **both wages** to remain safe this year.
Our **four-month reserve** covers a household repair, not retirement.
do: **Compare** registrations with receipts under senior review.
**Use** AI only for test ideas without member or card data.
feel: **Calm** about current work, with retirement figures still unknown.
S0.quote: A child should not be turned away from practice because a screen forgot a fee.
fieldNote: She checks **member receipts** with volunteers and a senior despite occasional AI test ideas.
Two steady wages and **four months saved** make the present situation secure.

steps.text: Keep checking club registrations against receipts with senior review
Transfer 100 monthly to savings while both wages arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office Steady Disruption can write and check booking code faster, while robots in garden-tool repair come later. I would ask the clubs to test new payment flows before we cut the volunteer’s help desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think junior coding hours may shrink, including mine. I will use a tool when it proves itself, but I cannot replace a lost wage with confidence in a demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for a paid afternoon to learn how to test AI-written booking code in our sandbox, with a senior checking the results. I’d take it only if the paid time is approved and no member data enters the tool. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d search actual club-support openings that state pay and keep Ben’s usual wage in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours. We have four months to look, but the mortgage still needs two wages for comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you test in the sandbox?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A coach once used a discount code twice and the system charged the family twice. I would use that case to test whether an AI draft spots duplicate payment paths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would club support pay enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben would keep his repair hours while the workshop offers them. I would not assume a new club-support post pays as much as software until I see the wage.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach booking code before workshop robots.
I would keep **club-tested payment flows** before reducing volunteer help.
think: I expect my **junior hours** could shrink.
I require **proof in the sandbox** before trusting an AI draft.
do: **Learn** AI-code testing only in approved paid sandbox time with senior review and no member data.
**Search** real club-support openings with stated wages if developer hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours, with four months to search.
S1.quote: I cannot replace a lost wage with confidence in a demo.
fieldNote: Her **AI learning** is a specific sandbox test with approved paid time and privacy limits.
A **club-support search** begins only if her hours fall, with actual pay to check.

steps.text: Learn AI-code testing only with approved paid sandbox time, senior review and no member data
Search real club-support openings with stated wages if junior hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could do our software thinking work in 2028; garden-tool repair robots arrive around 2031. Ben may still repair tools by hand for a while, but his booking and parts orders may change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my junior post could go quickly. Four months saved is useful, but there are only some local jobs and other firms may cut code at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written layoff terms and keep our reserve for mortgage payments. I’d cancel our planned holiday booking before a deposit is due. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible income help; I would not treat Ben’s possible overtime as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my wage before a replacement exists. I could make calls. The holiday deposit is easier to stop than a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children the family trip must wait. I would not ask them to pay for a trip we cannot afford ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Ben’s work carry the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben’s workshop orders might hold while people still repair old tools. We would count only his actual paid hours, not the hope that robots arrive late.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach code before 2031 repair robots.
I would say **parts ordering** changes before tool repair does.
think: I expect my **junior post** could go quickly.
I cannot assume **other software firms** will hire after full thinking AI.
do: **Request** written layoff terms and hold reserve for mortgage.
**Cancel** planned family holiday before its deposit is due.
**Apply** to real paid openings and eligible income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about wage loss before another job exists.
S2.quote: The holiday deposit is easier to stop than a mortgage payment.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 code loss** before garden-tool robots around 2031.
She cancels a **family trip** and holds cash for housing without assuming Ben’s overtime or children’s pay.

steps.text: Request written layoff terms, cancel family holiday before deposit and protect mortgage reserve
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible public income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches booking code in 2031 and garden-tool robots around 2034. Five years gives us time to learn whether the empty bedroom could bring in real rent, not just an advert’s estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer coding hours. Renting a room could help with the mortgage, but Ben and I would lose privacy and I do not know if local rules permit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the housing office what rules apply and get a written rental estimate for our spare room. Ben and I would rent it only if he agrees, the rules allow it, a checked tenant signs a lease, and rent after costs actually helps the mortgage. In the first year after 2031, if my code wage ends, we would continue only while the lease pays and our household is comfortable; I would also apply to actual paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the code wage, but five years allows us to test the numbers and the family cost. A lodger is a person in our kitchen, not a line in a budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would family visits change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter sometimes sleeps in that room when visiting. I would ask her how she feels, but Ben and I would decide together whether rent is worth changing those visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which costs belong in the rental figure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the room income after tax, utilities and any safety work. I will not buy furniture on the strength of a listing with no tenant.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 tool robots.
I would test **actual room rent** before treating it as mortgage help.
think: I expect **coding hours** could shrink when full thinking AI reaches club software.
I know a **lodger** would change our privacy and grown children’s visits.
do: **Check** rental rules and written net estimate for spare room.
**Rent** only with Ben’s agreement, legal permission, checked tenant and signed cost-covering lease.
**Continue** after 2031 code-wage loss only while signed rent pays and our household remains comfortable; apply to real openings.
feel: **Anxious** about wage loss and household privacy.
S3.quote: A lodger is a person in our kitchen, not a line in a budget.
fieldNote: Her **room-rental plan** requires legal permission, Ben’s agreement and a checked, signed tenant.
She measures **net rent** after costs and family visits; it cannot be presumed to replace code pay.

steps.text: Rent spare room only with permission, Ben’s agreement, signed tenant and positive net rent
Continue room lease after 2031 coding loss only while rent pays and household stays comfortable
Apply to actual paid openings if code wage ends after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends AGI by 2036 puts booking code under pressure in 2036; hands-on tool robots follow around 2039. A decade lets us measure whether work and savings actually make retirement possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my wage is safe for now, but junior hours might fall before 2036. I would not promise retirement just because I will be older; we need written income figures and the remaining mortgage balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking club payments and save 100 monthly while both wages hold. Ben and I would request our actual retirement statements and mortgage balance every year. In the first year after 2036, if my code job ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if verified income and savings cover housing and living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later junior cuts, though we can pay the mortgage now. Time helps us check actual figures without rushing the children into paying for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rent the room now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave the spare room for family visits unless a real rental arrangement passed all those checks. A future room listing does not pay this month’s bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our children about their own plans, not their wages. They owe us a visit, perhaps, but not a mortgage payment.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 repair robots.
I would check **written retirement figures** against the mortgage.
think: I expect my **current wage** to hold for now while people check club payments.
I worry **junior hours** may fall before 2036 even with a longer warning.
do: **Keep** checking club fees and save 100 monthly while both wages hold.
**Request** annual retirement and mortgage statements with Ben.
**Seek** real paid work after 2036 if coding ends; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Uneasy** about later cuts, with current mortgage payments secure.
S4.quote: A future room listing does not pay this month’s bill.
fieldNote: Her **retirement decision** depends on personal written figures, not age or adult children’s pay.
The **spare room** stays for family unless a real legal, agreed rental arrangement passes earlier gates.

steps.text: Keep checking club fees against receipts while employed
Save 100 monthly while both wages hold
After 2036 coding loss, seek work; retire only if verified resources cover housing and living costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior wage could go before we test another income. Written terms, a real paid opening, and eligible support would help. Four months saved is breathing space, not a retirement plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the volunteer at the sports-club door whether the paid list matches the families standing there. A missing fee can look like a missing child.

headlineQuote: A missing fee can look like a missing child.
portrait: Hana is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and four months saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** for test ideas, checking sports-club fees against actual receipts and senior review.
Her husband’s **garden-tool repair** income is steady; they have a mortgage and grown children.
She considers **spare-room rent** only with legal permission, Ben’s agreement, a signed tenant and positive net income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior wage before another income is tested.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, a real paid opening and eligible income support would help.
